[THOUGHT] 
This 33-year-old woman reports genuine, functionally limiting muscle weakness and extreme fatigue. Basic screening excludes common systemic causes of fatigue/weakness such as anemia and hypothyroidism, and pregnancy is negative. True neuromuscular weakness severe enough to impair self-care in a young woman most commonly reflects a neuromuscular junction disorder or primary myopathy. Among these, generalized myasthenia gravis (MG) is a leading consideration in this demographic: MG classically affects young women, causes true, often activity-worsened (fatigable) weakness that can be generalized and severe, and commonly has normal routine labs (CBC, TSH). Ocular signs (ptosis/diplopia) may be absent early or in some patients, so their absence does not exclude MG. Primary inflammatory myopathies (polymyositis/dermatomyositis) are also possible but typically show elevated CK and more insidious proximal weakness; those data are not provided. The single objective findings (normal CBC, normal TSH, negative urine hCG) neither confirm nor meaningfully increase the likelihood of MG. [FEEDBACK] To support or refute generalized myasthenia gravis, obtain the following critical information and tests:
- Detailed targeted history: onset and time course, fatigability pattern (worse with exertion/throughout the day, improves with rest), diurnal variation, presence/absence of ptosis or diplopia, bulbar symptoms (dysphagia, dysarthria), respiratory symptoms (dyspnea, orthopnea), medication exposures, recent infections, and any prior autoimmune disease.
- Focused neurologic and general exam: cranial nerves (ptosis, eye movements, facial weakness), detailed proximal vs distal limb strength with repetitive or sustained maneuvers to demonstrate fatigability, reflexes, sensory exam, and assessment of bulbar and respiratory function (including bedside vital capacity/oxygenation).
- Medication list, pregnancy status confirmed (urine test already negative but document), past medical history, and social/family history.
- Laboratory and diagnostic testing: serum acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibodies and MuSK (and LRP4 if available); creatine kinase (to evaluate myopathy); basic metabolic panel and inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP) as indicated.
- Electrophysiology: repetitive nerve stimulation and/or single-fiber EMG.
- Chest imaging (CT or MRI) to evaluate for thymoma if MG suspected.
- If any signs of respiratory compromise, obtain urgent pulmonary function tests (FVC) and consider urgent admission.

Collect these data before accepting or rejecting generalized myasthenia gravis as the working diagnosis.
